claim: Metastatic breast cancer is the second leading cause of cancer-related death among women in the United States.
source: In the United States, metastatic breast cancer is the second leading cause of cancer-related death among women (Harbeck et al., 2019; Torre et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harbeck et al., 2019 and Torre et al., 2017

claim: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) has the worst prognosis among all breast cancer subtypes.
source: In particular, triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) has the worst prognosis among all breast cancer subtypes, largely owing to its high metastatic proclivity to the lungs and other sites and because there are few effective treatments against this disease once it has metastasized (Al-Mahmood et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Al-Mahmood et al., 2018

claim: TNBC has high metastatic proclivity to the lungs and other sites.
source: In particular, triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) has the worst prognosis among all breast cancer subtypes, largely owing to its high metastatic proclivity to the lungs and other sites and because there are few effective treatments against this disease once it has metastasized (Al-Mahmood et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Al-Mahmood et al., 2018

claim: Patients with BRCA1/2 mutations or high programmed death-ligand 1 account for only 9.3–15.4% of TNBC cases.
source: However, these patients account for only 9.3–15.4% of TNBC cases (Armstrong et al., 2019), and new treatment strategies are urgently needed.
evidence: Supported by citation to Armstrong et al., 2019

claim: Tumor growth is modulated by reversible epigenetic mechanisms.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that tumor growth is modulated by reversible epigenetic mechanisms (Blair and Yan, 2012; Cao et al., 2014; Cao and Yan, 2013; Chen and Yan, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Blair and Yan, 2012; Cao et al., 2014; Cao and Yan, 2013; Chen and Yan, 2021

claim: Distinct chromatin states in primary human breast cancers distinguish established molecular subtypes and correlate with metastatic relapse and poor clinical outcome.
source: In primary human breast cancers, we and others recently identified distinct chromatin states, which distinguish established molecular subtypes and correlate with metastatic relapse and poor clinical outcome (Cai et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cai et al., 2020

claim: KMT2 family protein complexes mark active promoters and enhancers with histone H3 lysine K4 (H3K4) methylation.
source: Epigenetic regulators that are known to be involved in tumorigenesis include the KMT2 (also known as MLL/SET1) family protein complexes which mark active promoters and enhancers with histone H3 lysine K4 (H3K4) methylation and the non-specific lethal (NSL) complex which acetylates histones (Dias et al., 2014; Raja et al., 2010; Ruthenburg et al., 2007; Wysocka et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dias et al., 2014; Raja et al., 2010; Ruthenburg et al., 2007; Wysocka et al., 2005

claim: The NSL complex acetylates histones.
source: Epigenetic regulators that are known to be involved in tumorigenesis include the KMT2 (also known as MLL/SET1) family protein complexes which mark active promoters and enhancers with histone H3 lysine K4 (H3K4) methylation and the non-specific lethal (NSL) complex which acetylates histones (Dias et al., 2014; Raja et al., 2010; Ruthenburg et al., 2007; Wysocka et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dias et al., 2014; Raja et al., 2010; Ruthenburg et al., 2007; Wysocka et al., 2005

claim: WDR5 is a WD40 repeat protein that is a scaffold for the assembly of the KMT2 and NSL complexes.
source: WDR5 is a WD40 repeat protein that is a scaffold for the assembly of the KMT2 and NSL complexes (Guarnaccia and Tansey, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guarnaccia and Tansey, 2018

claim: WDR5 physically interacts with the proto-oncogene and transcription factor MYC to guide its chromatin binding and transcriptional activation.
source: More recently, WDR5 was found to physically interact with the proto-oncogene and transcription factor MYC to guide its chromatin binding and transcriptional activation, suggesting that WDR5 is a tractable target for MYC-driven cancers (Thomas et al., 2015a; Thomas et al., 2015b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Thomas et al., 2015a; Thomas et al., 2015b

claim: Aberrant WDR5 expression may occur in a number of cancer types.
source: Aberrant WDR5 expression itself may occur in a number of cancer types (Chen et al., 2015; Dai et al., 2015; Ge et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2015; Dai et al., 2015; Ge et al., 2016

claim: WDR5 may contribute to tumor sphere formation and cell proliferation.
source: Biologically, WDR5 may contribute to tumor sphere formation and cell proliferation (Carugo et al., 2016; Chung et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carugo et al., 2016; Chung et al., 2016

claim: WDR5 broadly regulates the expression of ribosomal protein (RP) genes across multiple cell lines and cancer types.
source: On the other hand, WDR5 was recently discovered to broadly regulate the expression of ribosomal protein (RP) genes across multiple cell lines and cancer types (Aho et al., 2019; Bryan et al., 2020; Guarnaccia et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aho et al., 2019; Bryan et al., 2020; Guarnaccia et al., 2021

claim: Deregulation of RP gene expression and translation has been implicated in breast cancer metastasis.
source: Moreover, deregulation of RP gene expression and translation has been implicated in breast cancer metastasis (Ebright et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ebright et al., 2020

claim: An in vivo screening platform identified WDR5 as a key regulator of breast cancer cell growth and metastatic colonization.
source: Here, we established an in vivo screening platform that identified WDR5 as a key regulator of breast cancer cell growth and metastatic colonization.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study described in the manuscript

claim: WDR5 regulates RP gene expression and global protein translation independently of the KMT2 complex.
source: We further showed that WDR5 regulates RP gene expression and global protein translation independently of the KMT2 complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study described in the manuscript

claim: WDR5 inhibition or degradation could be used as a therapeutic approach for TNBC.
source: Moreover, our results indicate that WDR5 inhibition or degradation could be used as a therapeutic approach for TNBC and that WDR5 targeting could be combined with mTOR inhibitors to achieve significant therapeutic benefit.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study described in the manuscript

claim: WDR5 targeting could be combined with mTOR inhibitors to achieve significant therapeutic benefit.
source: Moreover, our results indicate that WDR5 inhibition or degradation could be used as a therapeutic approach for TNBC and that WDR5 targeting could be combined with mTOR inhibitors to achieve significant therapeutic benefit.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study described in the manuscript

claim: The in vivo screen identified 14 significant hits with 7 drop-out hits and 7 enrichment hits.
source: From the in vivo screen, we identified 14 significant hits (p<0.05, log2FC >0.8 or log2FC <−0.8, FC:+DOX/−DOX), and among these, 7 were drop-out hits where shRNA representation significantly decreased, while 7 were enrichment hits where shRNA representation significantly increased (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1b

claim: Many in vivo drop-out candidates were also drop-out candidates in vitro.
source: Many of these in vivo drop-out candidates were drop-out candidates in vitro (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1b

claim: The screen identified drop-out shRNAs against MCM6, an essential eukaryotic genome replication factor.
source: For example, our screen identified drop-out shRNAs against MCM6, an essential eukaryotic genome replication factor, and CSNK2A1, previously shown to enhance metastatic growth of MDA-MB-231 cells (Bae et al., 2016; Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B and C, and citation to Bae et al., 2016

claim: The screen identified drop-out shRNAs against CSNK2A1, previously shown to enhance metastatic growth of MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: For example, our screen identified drop-out shRNAs against MCM6, an essential eukaryotic genome replication factor, and CSNK2A1, previously shown to enhance metastatic growth of MDA-MB-231 cells (Bae et al., 2016; Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B and C, and citation to Bae et al., 2016

claim: WDR5 can be inhibited by small molecules.
source: Among the top hits and potential therapeutic targets that were identified, we focused on WDR5 because it can be inhibited by small molecules, and shWDR5 was the second most significantly depleted shRNA in vivo (after shMCM6).
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about WDR5

claim: shWDR5 was the second most significantly depleted shRNA in vivo (after shMCM6).
source: Among the top hits and potential therapeutic targets that were identified, we focused on WDR5 because it can be inhibited by small molecules, and shWDR5 was the second most significantly depleted shRNA in vivo (after shMCM6).
evidence: This is a finding from the screen described in the manuscript

claim: WDR5 is known canonically as a scaffolding protein that recognizes and binds to methylated H3K4.
source: WDR5 is known canonically as a scaffolding protein that recognizes and binds to methylated H3K4, allowing the modification of H3K4 trimethylation by the KMT2 protein complex (Wysocka et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wysocka et al., 2005

claim: WDR5 allows the modification of H3K4 trimethylation by the KMT2 protein complex.
source: WDR5 is known canonically as a scaffolding protein that recognizes and binds to methylated H3K4, allowing the modification of H3K4 trimethylation by the KMT2 protein complex (Wysocka et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wysocka et al., 2005

claim: WDR5 has been implicated in the growth of metastatic breast cancer cells.
source: WDR5 has also been implicated in the growth of metastatic breast cancer cells, although the mechanism underlying this function of WDR5 is not clearly delineated (Punzi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Punzi et al., 2019

claim: Both shRNAs against WDR5 caused a significant but modest decrease in cell proliferation when compared to a control shRNA over 5 days.
source: Following 3 days of shRNA induction in vitro (Figure 1D), both shRNAs against WDR5 caused a significant but modest decrease in cell proliferation when compared to a control shRNA (shCtrl) over 5 days (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D and 1E

claim: WDR5 knockdown had a profound impact on the in vitro clonogenic ability of LM2 cells over 9 days.
source: In addition, using long-term in vitro colony formation assays over 9 days, we found a profound impact of WDR5 knockdown on the in vitro clonogenic ability of LM2 cells (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F and G

claim: WDR5 knockdown significantly impaired lung colonization by LM2 cells as early as day 7 post-injection.
source: We observed a significant impairment on lung colonization by LM2 cells as early as day 7 post-injection (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1H and I

claim: At day 50, the average lung metastatic burden in mice with shWDR5 cells was 5.7- or 16.5-fold lower than that in mice with LM2 cells expressing the control shRNA.
source: At the end point (day 50), the average lung metastatic burden in the mice with shWDR5 cells was 5.7- or 16.5-fold lower than that in mice with LM2 cells expressing the control shRNA (Figure 1H and J).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1H and J

claim: Knockdown of WDR5 significantly decreased mammary tumor growth in the shWDR5 group compared to control tumors.
source: We observed a significant decrease in mammary tumor growth in the shWDR5 group compared to control tumors (Figure 1K and L, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F-H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1K, L, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F-H

claim: An even larger decrease in lung and liver metastasis from the mammary fat pad tumors was observed in the shWDR5 group compared to shCtrl.
source: Notably, we observed an even larger decrease in lung and liver metastasis from the mammary fat pad tumors in the shWDR5 group as compared to shCtrl, which suggests a potential metastasis-specific function of WDR5 (compare Figure 1—figure supplement 1I-J to Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H, I, and J

claim: WDR5 is independently required for the cellular outgrowth, tumorigenic, and lung colonizing capacities of LM2 TNBC cells.
source: Taken together, we showed that WDR5 is independently required for the cellular outgrowth, tumorigenic, and lung colonizing capacities of LM2 TNBC cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript

claim: WDR5 knockdown significantly reduced the clonogenic outgrowth of all tested breast cancer cell lines spanning three established molecular subtypes.
source: WDR5 knockdown significantly reduced the clonogenic outgrowth of all the tested cell lines (Figure 2B and C), suggesting that WDR5 enhances tumor cell growth across multiple breast cancer subtypes.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B and C

claim: WDR5 enhances tumor cell growth across multiple breast cancer subtypes.
source: WDR5 knockdown significantly reduced the clonogenic outgrowth of all the tested cell lines (Figure 2B and C), suggesting that WDR5 enhances tumor cell growth across multiple breast cancer subtypes.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing WDR5 knockdown effects across multiple cell lines

claim: OICR-9429 is a small molecule antagonist of the WDR5-KMT2 interaction.
source: We next tested the efficacy of a known WDR5 inhibitor, OICR-9429, which is a small molecule antagonist of the WDR5-KMT2 interaction (Grebien et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grebien et al., 2015

claim: Treatment of LM2 cells with OICR-9429 at 20 μM for 9 days significantly reduced their colony formation ability.
source: We treated LM2 cells with OICR-9429 at 20 μM for 9 days, and this also significantly reduced their colony formation ability (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D and E

claim: MS67 led to WDR5 degradation at a concentration as low as 0.02 μM.
source: We found that MS67, but not the negative control MS67N, which does not bind to CRBN, nor OICR-9429, induced WDR5 degradation at a concentration as low as 0.02 μM (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: At 2.5 μM MS67, approximately 80% WDR5 degradation was achieved in LM2 cells and approximately 70% degradation in MDA-MB-453 cells.
source: Specifically, at 2.5 μM MS67, we achieved ~80% WDR5 degradation in LM2 cells and ~70% of degradation in MDA-MB-453 cells (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: The maximal WDR5 degradation by MS67 can be achieved at 8 hr post-treatment and remains stable for 72 hr in both LM2 and MDA-MB-453 cells.
source: Additionally, the maximal degradation can be achieved at 8 hr post-treatment, and this effect remains stable for 72 hr in both LM2 and MDA-MB-453 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E

claim: MS67 leads to approximately 50% growth inhibition at 0.5 μM and approximately 80% inhibition at 2.5 μM.
source: We found that MS67 leads to ~50% growth inhibition at 0.5 μM and ~80% inhibition at 2.5 μM (Figure 2I and J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2I, J, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and G

claim: The effect of 2.5 μM MS67 treatment is comparable to shRNA knockdown and more potent than 20 μM OICR-9429 treatment in LM2 and MDA-MB-453 cells.
source: Importantly, the effect of 2.5 μM MS67 treatment is comparable to shRNA knockdown and more potent than 20 μM OICR-9429 treatment in LM2 and MDA-MB-453 cells, while 2.5 μM of OICR-9429 treatment only caused a modest effect (compare Figures 1F, G, 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: Supported by comparison of data shown in Figures 1F, G, 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and G

claim: MS67-mediated WDR5 degradation showed improved growth inhibition of breast cancer cells when compared to the OICR-9429 compound.
source: In summary, MS67-mediated WDR5 degradation showed improved growth inhibition of breast cancer cells when compared to the OICR-9429 compound.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript

claim: Inhibition of WDR5 led to more down-regulated genes than up-regulated genes.
source: In general, inhibition of WDR5 led to more down-regulated genes than up-regulated genes, which supports previous findings that WDR5 generally promotes transcriptional activation (Wysocka et al., 2005; Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A and citation to Wysocka et al., 2005

claim: WDR5 generally promotes transcriptional activation.
source: In general, inhibition of WDR5 led to more down-regulated genes than up-regulated genes, which supports previous findings that WDR5 generally promotes transcriptional activation (Wysocka et al., 2005; Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wysocka et al., 2005

claim: Certain DEGs were preferentially regulated in LM2, BrM3, or BoM cells, suggesting that WDR5 can regulate genes in a manner that is dependent on the metastatic proclivities of different breast cancer cell subpopulations.
source: Certain DEGs were preferentially regulated in LM2, BrM3, or BoM cells, suggesting that WDR5 can regulate genes in a manner that is dependent on the metastatic proclivities of different breast cancer cell subpopulations (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B

claim: 264 down-regulated and 118 up-regulated DEGs were shared across all three organotropic-metastatic cell subpopulations.
source: On the other hand, we also found DEGs (264 down-regulated and 118 up-regulated) that were shared across all lines (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 1c), indicative of some conserved WDR5 function across metastatic breast cancer cells.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 1c

claim: The most enriched and significant gene ontology in the shared down-regulated DEGs was cytoplasmic RPs.
source: We then performed Enrichr analysis on both the up- or down-regulated DEGs and found that the most enriched and significant gene ontology in the shared down-regulated DEGs was cytoplasmic RPs (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and Supplementary file 1d

claim: The combined score for cytoplasmic RPs enrichment was 18-fold higher than the next enriched ontology for the shared down-regulated DEGs.
source: The combined score for this enrichment was 18-fold higher than the next enriched ontology for the shared down-regulated DEGs, demonstrating the significance of this WDR5 regulated pathway (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1d

claim: Among the 474 down-regulated DEGs in LM2 cells, 51 (11%) encoded for RP genes.
source: Notably, among the 474 down-regulated DEGs in LM2 cells, 51 (11%) encoded for RP genes (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3D

claim: WDR5 knockdown with both hairpins for 3 days in LM2 cells confirmed down-regulation of all tested RP genes.
source: After inducing WDR5 knockdown with both hairpins for 3 days in LM2 cells, we confirmed down-regulation of all the tested RP genes. These included the top two down-regulated RPs, RPL7 and RPL31, which were consistently reduced by a ~50% (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Treatment of LM2 and MDA-MB-453 cells with 10 or 20 μM of OICR-9429 for 3 days decreased RPL7 and other RP genes.
source: Treatment of LM2 and MDA-MB-453 cells with 10 or 20 μM of OICR-9429 for 3 days decreased RPL7 and other RP genes as predicted (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D

claim: MS67 treatment at 2.5 μM significantly down-regulated several RP genes whereas OICR-9429 and MS67N did not have as significant of an effect at these lower concentrations.
source: MS67 treatment at 2.5 μM significantly down-regulate several RP genes whereas OICR-9429 and MS67N did not have as significant of an effect at these lower concentrations (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E

claim: WDR5 silencing impaired global protein translation rates.
source: Accordingly, WDR5 silencing impaired global protein translation rates (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F

claim: OICR-9429 treatment or MS67-mediated degradation caused decreases in protein translation in both LM2 and MDA-MB-453 cell lines.
source: OICR-9429 treatment or MS67-mediated degradation also caused decreases in protein translation in both LM2 and MDA-MB-453 cell lines (Figure 3I and J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3I, J, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G

claim: Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of WDR5 can suppress RP gene expression and global translation in breast cancer cells.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrates that either genetic or pharmacological inhibition of WDR5 can suppress RP gene expression and global translation in breast cancer cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript

claim: KMT2A binding to the WIN site can be disrupted by point mutation F133A on WDR5.
source: KMT2A binding to the WIN site can be disrupted by point mutation F133A on WDR5 (Guarnaccia et al., 2021; Patel et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guarnaccia et al., 2021 and Patel et al., 2008

claim: RBBP5 and c-MYC bind at the WBM site, which can be disrupted by point mutations N225A and V268E.
source: On the other hand, RBBP5 and c-MYC have been shown to bind at the WBM site, which can be disrupted by point mutations N225A and V268E (Guarnaccia et al., 2021; Thomas et al., 2015b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guarnaccia et al., 2021 and Thomas et al., 2015b

claim: WDR5 mutants K7Q and 1-25Δ were shown to specifically impact ciliogenesis.
source: In addition to the F133A, N225A, and V268E mutants, WDR5 mutants K7Q and 1-25Δ were recently shown to specifically impact ciliogenesis (Kulkarni et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kulkarni et al., 2018

claim: The F133A mutation abrogates the binding of WDR5 to KMT2A.
source: Using co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) assays, we observed that the F133A but not N25A or V268E mutations abrogate the binding of WDR5 to KMT2A.
evidence: Supported by Co-IP data described in the manuscript

claim: Mutants N225A and V268E reduced the binding of WDR5 to RBBP5 by more than 50%.
source: In contrast, mutants N225A and V268E but not F133A reduced the binding of WDR5 to RBBP5 by more than 50% as expected (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Expression of WT WDR5 rescued the growth defect caused by WDR5 knockdown.
source: Consistently, shWDR5 cells expressing GFP control had severely impacted colony formation, while expression of WT WDR5 rescued this growth defect (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4E and F

claim: The WIN site mutant F133A was able to rescue the colony formation phenotype caused by WDR5 knockdown.
source: Surprisingly, the WIN site mutant F133A was able to rescue the colony formation phenotype, while neither N225A nor V268E effectively rescued cell growth.
evidence: Supported by colony formation data described in the manuscript

claim: Neither N225A nor V268E effectively rescued cell growth after WDR5 knockdown.
source: Surprisingly, the WIN site mutant F133A was able to rescue the colony formation phenotype, while neither N225A nor V268E effectively rescued cell growth.
evidence: Supported by colony formation data described in the manuscript

claim: The WBM but not the WIN-binding ability of WDR5 is required for WDR5-dependent growth of TNBC cells.
source: These results suggest that the WBM but not the WIN-binding ability of WDR5 is required for WDR5-dependent growth of TNBC cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with WDR5 mutants

claim: The F133A mutant binds to the promoter of RPL7 and RPL31 less efficiently than WT WDR5.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation and qPCR (ChIP-qPCR) analysis showed that the F133A mutant binds to the promoter of RPL7 and RPL31 less efficiently, while N225A and V268E mutants bind chromatin similarly as the WT protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: N225A and V268E mutants bind chromatin similarly as the WT WDR5 protein.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation and qPCR (ChIP-qPCR) analysis showed that the F133A mutant binds to the promoter of RPL7 and RPL31 less efficiently, while N225A and V268E mutants bind chromatin similarly as the WT protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: All WDR5 mutants maintained a similar level of H3K4me3 at RP gene promoters.
source: Surprisingly, all mutants maintained a similar level of H3K4me3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that WDR5 binding to chromatin is not required for maintaining H3K4me3 at the RP gene promoters tested in this context.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: WDR5 binding to chromatin is not required for maintaining H3K4me3 at the RP gene promoters tested in LM2 cells.
source: Surprisingly, all mutants maintained a similar level of H3K4me3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that WDR5 binding to chromatin is not required for maintaining H3K4me3 at the RP gene promoters tested in this context.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-qPCR data showing similar H3K4me3 levels across mutants

claim: The N-terminal and F133A mutants rescued the expression of RP genes, whereas the N225A and V268E mutants did not.
source: More importantly, the N-terminal and F133A mutants rescued the expression of RP genes, whereas the N225A and V268E mutants did not (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4G

claim: In LM2 cells, WBM but not WIN binding by WDR5 is important for the maintenance of RP gene expression.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that, in LM2 cells, WBM but not WIN binding by WDR5 is important for the maintenance of RP gene expression.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the mutant rescue experiments

claim: Depleting KMT2A with multiple shRNAs did not reproducibly affect in vitro colony formation and in vivo lung metastasis growth.
source: However, depleting KMT2A with multiple shRNAs did not reproducibly affect in vitro colony formation and in vivo lung metastasis growth (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5D-F

claim: KMT2A is dispensable for WDR5-dependent cell growth.
source: This result is also consistent with the phenotype observed from the F133A mutant and suggests that KMT2A is dispensable for WDR5-dependent cell growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the KMT2A knockdown data and F133A mutant rescue data

claim: RP gene expression was not changed after knockdown of RBBP5, DPY30, or HCFC1.
source: RP gene expression was not changed after knockdown of RBBP5, DPY30, or HCFC1 (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5G

claim: Most KMT2 complex components are not required for the growth of LM2 cells.
source: Furthermore, most of these KMT2 complex components are not required for the growth of LM2 cells (Figure 5H and I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5H and I

claim: Knockdown of HCFC1 resulted in a 40% decrease in colony formation.
source: The exception was upon knockdown of HCFC1 which resulted in a 40% decrease in colony formation (Figure 5H and I), likely due to the role of HCFC1 in cell cycle control (Antonova et al., 2019; Xiang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5H and I, and citations to Antonova et al., 2019 and Xiang et al., 2020

claim: Knockdown of CXXC1, WDR82, or BOD1L1 did not decrease RP gene expression and colony formation.
source: However, knockdown of these components also did not decrease RP gene expression and colony formation (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5G-I

claim: The KMT2 complexes are not the major effectors of WDR5-dependent metastatic cell growth in the LM2 model.
source: Therefore, the KMT2 complexes are not the major effectors of WDR5-dependent metastatic cell growth in the LM2 model.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the KMT2 complex component knockdown experiments

claim: Treatment with OICR-9429 partially or completely blocked the adaptive induction of RP genes caused by mTOR inhibitors.
source: Interestingly, during the course of titrating mTOR inhibitors in our cell model, we noted that the treatment with OSI-027 or everolimus alone caused an up-regulation of RP gene expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-D), which may be due to an adaptive feedback effect on proteostasis following mTOR inhibition. Importantly, treatment with the WDR5 inhibitor OICR-9429 partially or completely blocked this adaptive induction of RP genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: mTOR inhibitors down-regulated phosphorylated S6 protein kinase (S6K) and translation initiation factor 4E binding protein 1 (4E-BP1).
source: Moreover, while mTOR inhibitors were confirmed to down-regulate phosphorylated S6 protein kinase (S6K) and translation initiation factor 4E binding protein 1 (4E-BP1), WDR5 inhibition reduced RP genes expression and translation independently of this signaling pathway (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F

claim: WDR5 inhibition reduced RP genes expression and translation independently of the mTOR signaling pathway.
source: Moreover, while mTOR inhibitors were confirmed to down-regulate phosphorylated S6 protein kinase (S6K) and translation initiation factor 4E binding protein 1 (4E-BP1), WDR5 inhibition reduced RP genes expression and translation independently of this signaling pathway (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F

claim: The overall translation was decreased when combining WDR5 inhibition or WDR5 knockdown with mTOR inhibition.
source: Next, we compared the global translation rates of LM2 or MDA-MB-453 cells, when WDR5 was inhibited genetically or pharmacologically in combination with mTOR inhibitors OSI-027 or everolimus. The overall translation was decreased when combining WDR5 inhibition or WDR5 knockdown with mTOR inhibition (Figure 6C and D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6C, D, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G

claim: Both OSI-027 and everolimus act synergistically with WDR5 inhibition in both LM2 and MDA-MB-453 cells.
source: Moreover, both OSI-027 and everolimus act synergistically with WDR5 inhibition in both LM2 and MDA-MB-453 cells (Figure 6E-L), while temsirolimus showed an additive effect in LM2 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1L and M).
